title: ANNUAL REPORT ON FORM 10-K FOR THE FISCAL YEAR ENDED JANUARY 31, 2023

References to Walmart Inc., Walmart, the Company, and related first-person terms mean the Delaware corporation and, unless otherwise specified or required by context, its consolidated subsidiaries; this definition applies to the report, incorporated proxy-statement information, and exhibits.

title: PART I

nodes.title: Cautionary Statement Regarding Forward-Looking Statements
nodes.summary: Walmart’s Form 10-K explains that its filings, announcements, and presentations may contain forward-looking statements protected by securities-law safe harbors. These are estimates, expectations, plans, or goals—not historical facts—and cover economic and market conditions; business growth and competition; financial and operating measures; investments, workforce, currency, shareholder returns, liquidity and cash flows; derivatives, taxes, regulation, litigation, accounting standards, and ESG commitments. Such statements may be identified by words like “expect,” “plan,” or “will,” rely on assumptions, and may differ materially from actual outcomes. Walmart cautions against undue reliance, says statements speak only as of their dates, and disclaims any duty to update them except as required by law.

nodes.title: ITEM 1. BUSINESS
The Development of Our Company
nodes.summary: Walmart describes itself as a people-led, technology-powered omnichannel retailer serving about 240 million customers weekly across more than 10,500 stores and eCommerce sites in 20 countries. Its strategy centers on convenience, disciplined operations, digital growth, culture, and trust, supported by everyday low prices and cost controls. It reports three segments, fiscal-year and consolidation practices, fiscal 2023 revenue of $611.3 billion, Bentonville headquarters, and NYSE ticker WMT. The text traces its development from 1945 variety stores through Sam’s Club, supercenters, international expansion, eCommerce, pickup and delivery, and investments including Flipkart and PhonePe. It highlights stores, technology, supply chains, associates, Walmart+, advertising, fulfillment, healthcare, and financial services as mutually reinforcing parts of its customer-focused growth strategy.

nodes.title: Information About Our Segments
nodes.summary: The company operates retail, wholesale, and other businesses, including eCommerce, across the U.S. and several international markets. It sold its Argentina operations in fiscal 2021 and its U.K. and Japan operations in fiscal 2022; related details are in Note 12. Its three reportable segments are Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam’s Club, each contributing differently to results. Segment contributions to net sales have generally remained consistent, with minor Walmart International changes due to market exits and currency fluctuations. Further segment and geographic information appears in Note 13.

nodes.title: Walmart U.S. Segment
nodes.summary: The text describes Walmart U.S. and International, covering their operating regions, formats, fiscal 2021–2023 sales and segment contributions, strategies, and portfolio changes. It details omnichannel services, membership and digital platforms, store sizes and locations, merchandise categories and private/licensed brands, other offerings, operations and seasonality, competitive pressures and responses, and distribution networks, facilities, suppliers, and eCommerce fulfillment. International coverage also includes country-specific businesses, financial and digital services, local sourcing, and market differences.

nodes.title: Sam's Club Segment
nodes.summary: Sam’s Club operates membership-only clubs in 44 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, plus samsclub.com, and reported fiscal 2023 sales of $84.3 billion (14% of consolidated sales), versus $73.6 billion in 2022 and $63.9 billion in 2021. Membership income is significant; the segment has lower gross margins and operating expenses than other segments. Club and Plus memberships cost $50 and $110 annually, respectively, with different add-on limits; both include a household card, while Plus adds shipping and prescription and glasses discounts. Sam’s Cash, launched in 2023, combines prior rewards and can be redeemed monthly in clubs or online, for fees, or as cash; it does not expire. The omni-channel business combines clubs, website, and apps through pickup, Scan & Go, shipping, and delivery; clubs average about 134,000 square feet. Five merchandise categories span groceries and consumables; fuel, tobacco, and other goods; home and apparel; health and wellness; and technology, office, and entertainment. Member’s Mark is expanding. Operations include 24-hour digital access, early shopping for Plus members, pickup at all clubs, and mobile checkout. Sales are seasonal, typically peaking in the quarter ending January 31. Competitors include warehouse clubs (especially Costco), retailers, grocers, wholesalers, fuel stations, and online and catalog sellers; value, assortment, bulk sizes, and digital channels support competition. Distribution uses 29 dedicated facilities, some Walmart facilities, direct supplier shipments, 13 eCommerce fulfillment centers, clubs, private trucks, and common carriers.

nodes.title: Intellectual Property
nodes.summary: The company considers its intellectual property important to its success and protects it through applicable laws, trade-secret protections, and confidentiality or license agreements. It has registered or sought registration of U.S. and international domain names, trademarks, service marks, and copyrights; filed patent applications for proprietary technology; and has licensed, and may continue to license, certain rights to third parties.

nodes.title: Supply Chain, Regulation and ESG Priorities
nodes.summary: The company relies on global and local suppliers to source merchandise, whose conduct must meet applicable labor, safety and other laws; sourcing, logistics and distribution affect product availability and assortment. Its global operations are subject to U.S. and foreign laws and regulations. Its ESG strategy seeks shared value and prioritizes opportunity, sustainability, community, and ethics and integrity, including inclusion, responsible sourcing, emissions and nature goals, community support, and trust. ESG disclosures may be updated and are not incorporated into SEC filings.

nodes.title: Human Capital Management
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its global workforce of approximately 2.1 million associates and its commitment to developing, rewarding, and retaining them as work and technology change. Its workforce strategy focuses on belonging, well-being, growth, and digital transformation. Initiatives include diversity and inclusion reporting, fair pay and associate feedback; competitive wages and benefits; career training through Walmart Academy and tuition-funded Live Better U; and digital tools, real-time feedback, and virtual healthcare. The text also provides workforce demographics, benefit details, reporting references, and a retirement-benefits disclosure.

nodes.summary: The text lists the Company’s executive officers as of the filing date of its Form 10-K, noting they are elected by and serve at the Board’s pleasure and that the stated experience generally reflects their principal occupations over the prior five years. nodes.title: Our Website and Availability of SEC Reports and Other Information
nodes.summary: Walmart’s website provides free access, as soon as reasonably practicable after SEC submission, to its SEC filings and shareholder documents; the SEC also makes electronic issuer filings available at sec.gov. SEC filings, senior financial officer reporting protocols, and the Code of Conduct are online and available in print on request from Investor Relations. Substantive amendments or waivers to the protocols or the CEO, CFO, or principal accounting officer’s Code of Conduct will be described under Corporate Governance on Walmart’s website for 12 months.

Describes Walmart’s history, omnichannel strategy, scale, financial reporting, headquarters and stock listing; its three segments, market exits, operations, sales, products, memberships, services, competition, seasonality and distribution; and its intellectual-property protections, supplier and regulatory environment, and ESG priorities. Covers workforce size, culture, pay, benefits, training and digital transformation; executive officers’ roles and experience; and access to SEC filings, shareholder information, reporting protocols and conduct-code disclosures.

nodes.title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS
Strategic and Consumer Trend Risks
key_items: Strategic Risks Failure to successfully execute our omni-channel strategy and the cost of our investments in eCommerce and technology may materially adversely affect our market position, net sales and financial performance.

If we do not timely identify or effectively respond to consumer trends or preferences, it could negatively affect our relationship with our customers, demand for the products and services we sell, our market share and the growth of our business.
nodes.summary: The filing warns that listed risks, which are not exhaustive, could materially harm business results, financial position, or liquidity. Failure to execute an omni-channel strategy and investments in eCommerce, technology, talent, automation, acquisitions, partnerships, and store initiatives could weaken market position, sales, and performance, cause asset impairments, or reduce store traffic and cross-sales; costs may hurt results before benefits emerge. Failure to anticipate or respond to changing consumer demand, shopping habits, priorities, and competitive factors—including price, assortment, convenience, shipping, and ESG preferences—could damage customer relationships, reputation, demand, market share, and growth.

nodes.title: We face strong competition from other retailers, wholesale club operators, omni-channel retailers, and other businesses which could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text warns that intense, rapidly changing competition across physical, eCommerce, omnichannel, wholesale, social commerce, and related services could harm financial results, especially if the company fails to respond, innovate, or execute its strategy; competitor consolidation and alliances may strengthen rivals. Domestic and international economic conditions—including prices, inflation, employment, credit, taxes, regulation, trade barriers, and recessions—could reduce demand, alter sales mix, increase costs, slow inventory turnover, cause markdowns or asset impairments, and disrupt suppliers. Strategic alliances, business relationships, and investments, including fintech, healthcare, and divested-market investments, may underperform or weaken the company’s competitive position.

nodes.title: Competitive, Economic, and Partnership Risks
key_items: General or macro-economic factors, both domestically and internationally, may materially adversely affect our financial performance.
The performance of strategic alliances and other business relationships to support the expansion of our business could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The company’s performance may suffer if it fails to respond to retail and digital competition, competitors’ innovations, or industry consolidation and alliances that strengthen rivals. Domestic and international economic conditions—including inflation, interest rates, energy and other costs, unemployment, consumer credit and spending, currency and tax changes, regulation, trade barriers, and recession—may weaken demand, shift sales toward lower-margin goods, slow inventory turnover, increase markdowns and expenses, impair assets, and disrupt suppliers. Strategic alliances and other business relationships may underperform expectations, weaken its competitive position, or make associated investments financially harmful.

nodes.title: Operational Risks Global or regional health pandemics or epidemics, including COVID-19, could negatively impact our business, financial position and results of operations.
nodes.summary: Pandemics or epidemics, including COVID-19 and future variants or outbreaks, may disrupt operations, product demand and availability, inventory planning, supply chains, transportation, costs, and the ability to forecast performance. Impacts depend on disease severity and duration, restrictions, vaccination and treatment effectiveness, economic conditions, recovery pace, and lasting changes in consumer behavior; they may cause shortages, delays, litigation exposure, and weaker financial results. Such events may also intensify risks involving competition, reputation, strategic initiatives, cybersecurity, payments, technology, labor, supply chains, and regulation.

nodes.title: Natural disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, global health epidemics or pandemics, catastrophic and other events could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks that disasters, extreme weather and climate change, geopolitical conflict, pandemics, violence, theft, and infrastructure or transport disruptions could damage facilities, interrupt operations and supply chains, alter customer behavior, raise costs, and materially harm performance, especially in the U.S. Climate risks include physical impacts and transition-related regulation, prices, and reputation. Supplier risks include instability, labor, compliance, quality, sourcing, trade, currency, and logistics problems. Unsafe products may cause customer losses, liability, and reputational damage; third-party marketplace sales also create legal, counterfeit, compliance, and enforcement risks that could undermine eCommerce and business results.

nodes.title: Climate, Supplier, and Product Risks
key_items: Risks associated with our suppliers could materially adversely affect our financial performance.

If the products we sell are not safe or otherwise fail to meet our customers' expectations, we could lose customers, incur liability for any injuries suffered by customers using or consuming a product we sell or otherwise experience a material impact to our brand, reputation and financial performance. We are also subject to reputational and other risks related to third-party sales on our digital platforms.
nodes.summary: Climate-related physical and transition events could disrupt operations, damage facilities or inventory, raise costs, and harm performance, especially in the U.S. Supplier instability, legal or standards failures, labor and material shortages, transport disruptions, currency, inflation, and trade restrictions could limit product access and hurt results. Unsafe or disappointing products may drive customers away, trigger liability claims, and damage reputation. Third-party marketplace sales also pose legal, compliance, counterfeit, prohibited-goods, financial, and reputational risks that could undermine eCommerce growth and business performance.

nodes.title: We rely extensively on information and financial systems to process transactions, summarize results and manage our business. Disruptions in our systems could harm our ability to conduct our operations.
nodes.summary: The company depends on information and financial systems for transactions and business management, making uninterrupted operation critical. Systems face risks from technical failures, cyberattacks, disasters, human error, unrest, and conflict; they are not fully redundant, and recovery plans cannot cover every event. Disruptions could require costly repairs, cause data loss, interrupt operations, and materially harm results. Technology updates add risk, and failed integration may forfeit expected benefits. A financial-system upgrade begun in fiscal 2024 could, if not implemented as planned, impair financial-reporting controls and their assessment, as well as reputation, business, financial condition, results, and cash flows.

nodes.title: If the technology-based systems that give our customers the ability to shop with us online and enable us to deliver products and services do not function effectively, our operating results, as well as our ability to grow our omni-channel business globally, could be materially adversely affected.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks that technology failures could undermine Walmart’s omnichannel growth, customer experience, sales, reputation, and operations. Digital platforms and third-party systems support online shopping, marketing, pickup, delivery, shipping, and supply-chain automation, but must keep pace with customer and competitor expectations. Platforms face cyberattacks that can steal data, disrupt services, shopping, and supply chains. The company stores sensitive customer, member, employee, vendor, and health information, relies on providers and public networks, and faces evolving threats, human error, software vulnerabilities, and remote-work risks. Breaches may go undetected and cause litigation, regulatory penalties, remediation costs, liability, operational and financial losses, and reputational harm; controls cannot eliminate all risk. Payment methods and financial services create security, industry-standard, privacy, consumer-finance, anti-money-laundering, and sanctions obligations, including breach-notification duties; noncompliance can bring fines and other consequences.

nodes.title: Changes in type or scope of offerings of our health and wellness business or the Walmart Health business could adversely affect our overall results of operations, cash flows and liquidity.
nodes.summary: Walmart’s pharmacy and health businesses—including retail pharmacies, Walmart Health centers, telehealth, and its UnitedHealth Group collaboration—face risks that could affect results, cash flows, and liquidity. Pharmacy risks include reimbursement, payer mix and formularies, network access, drug costs and supply, administrative burdens, product and customer mix, insurance and government programs, competition, consolidation, economic conditions, performance thresholds, financial-assistance rules, and regulatory changes. Health-clinic risks include reimbursement and contracts, payer mix, competition, care practices, value-based purchasing, patient ability to pay, staffing, regulation, technology, and public health. These factors may reduce sales, margins, service volumes, cross-selling, or the scope and pace of health-business expansion.

nodes.title: Our failure to attract and retain qualified associates, increases in wage and benefit costs, changes in laws and other labor issues could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart’s operations and financial performance depend on attracting and retaining qualified associates, controlling wage and benefit costs, staffing locations, and managing organizational and leadership transitions. Labor availability, competition from retail and other industries, demographics, insurance costs, and changes in labor or healthcare laws may raise costs or hinder recruitment and service, materially harming results. Separately, because stock prices reflect high expectations, missing or delaying targets for sales, income, spending, comparable-store and eCommerce growth, margins, or earnings—or changes to dividends, repurchases, tax rates, analyst estimates, or relative retailer performance—could lower the stock price and increase volatility.

nodes.title: Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may materially adversely affect our financial performance and our reported results of operations.
nodes.summary: Unfavorable foreign-exchange movements can distort translated results, hurt Walmart International and consolidated performance, and raise costs of imported goods when selling prices cannot be adjusted, reducing gross profit. International operations—about 17% of fiscal 2023 net sales across Africa, Canada, Central America, Chile, China, India and Mexico—face political, economic, legal, regulatory, tax, labor, trade, currency, competition, product-safety, environmental, consumer/data-protection and other country-specific risks, including instability, inflation, devaluation, restrictions, nationalization and enforcement difficulties. Managing diverse jurisdictions also creates operational, tax and intellectual-property challenges. Associates, contractors or agents may violate anti-corruption laws despite company policies and compliance programs, potentially harming business, finances and reputation.

nodes.title: Changes in tax and trade laws and regulations could materially adversely affect our financial performance.
nodes.summary: Walmart warns that changes in trade policies, tariffs, and regulations could raise merchandise costs and selling prices, harming its business and financial performance; its U.S. and Sam’s Club segments generated about 83% of fiscal 2023 net sales, and much U.S. general merchandise is sourced abroad. Worldwide taxes are affected by earnings mix, estimates of deferred tax assets and liabilities, and evolving laws, rates, regulations, accounting rules, and interpretations. The Tax Act and new tax requirements may increase compliance costs. OECD Pillar Two and other international reforms, including a 15% country-by-country minimum tax, could materially affect its effective tax rate. Tax authorities regularly audit Walmart, and final tax outcomes may differ materially from recorded estimates, affecting tax expense, net income, or cash flows.

nodes.title: Changes in and/or failure to comply with other laws, regulations, and interpretations of such laws and regulations specific to the businesses and jurisdictions in which we operate could materially adversely affect our reputation, market position, or our business and financial performance.
nodes.summary: The text explains that changing or failing to meet complex U.S. and international laws could harm the company’s reputation, operations, market position, and financial results. It covers healthcare and pharmacy regulation; controlled substances, reimbursement, fraud and abuse, and pricing reforms; general rules on competition, products, labor, environment, financial services, sanctions, and ESG; and extensive privacy, cybersecurity, and communications requirements. New rules, enforcement, scrutiny, audits, or investigations may require costly changes and trigger fines, litigation, license or program losses, contract termination, and other penalties.

nodes.title: We are subject to risks related to litigation and other legal proceedings that may materially adversely affect our results of operations, financial position and liquidity.
nodes.summary: The company faces potentially costly, disruptive legal proceedings and government investigations that could materially harm its operations, financial position, liquidity, or cash flows. Matters include wage-and-hour and consumer class actions; opioid dispensing and distribution investigations and litigation, with losses not estimable; an Indian foreign-investment notice concerning pre-acquisition Flipkart conduct; and FTC litigation and DOJ inquiries into money-transfer services, fraud prevention, and anti-money-laundering compliance. Outcomes and impacts are uncertain, and further cases may arise. The bylaws generally make Delaware’s Court of Chancery the exclusive forum for specified shareholder claims, potentially raising costs, discouraging claims, or prompting added costs if unenforceable; federal securities-law jurisdiction is unaffected.

nodes.title: Our reputation may be adversely affected if we are not able to achieve our ESG goals.
nodes.summary: The company’s ESG aspirations and goals reflect stakeholder expectations and are periodically reported on its website, but achieving them involves risks and factors beyond its control. Stakeholders may be dissatisfied with its goals or progress, and it may fail—or be perceived to fail—to meet them. ESG challenges are discussed in reporting that is not part of or incorporated into the Form 10-K. Actual or perceived failure could harm the company’s reputation, associate morale, and customer or shareholder support.

The section warns that numerous non-exhaustive risks could materially harm Walmart’s business, financial condition, results, liquidity, cash flows, reputation, or stock price. These include failure to execute its omnichannel, technology, investment, acquisition, partnership, and health-business strategies; changing consumer preferences and intense competition; economic downturns, inflation, currency movements, and changing trade, tax, and other laws; pandemics, disasters, climate change, geopolitical events, supplier, product-safety, and marketplace risks; information-system, technology, cybersecurity, privacy, and payment failures; labor shortages and rising costs; international operating and compliance challenges; litigation and government investigations; and failure to achieve ESG goals or meet market expectations.

title: ITEM 3. LEGAL PROCEEDINGS

It also describes an early-stage Indian foreign-investment notice involving Flipkart, with outcome uncertain, and California hazardous-waste enforcement litigation scheduled for trial in 2024, which Walmart contests and could entail over $1 million in penalties. nodes.title: ITEM 7. MANAGEMENT'S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: The MD&A explains its coverage of fiscal 2021–2023 results, financial statements, performance metrics, and segment results. It defines segment operating income, comparable sales—including eCommerce, exclusions, and calculation limits—and currency effects. It summarizes strategic portfolio actions and related losses: sales of Argentina, Asda, and Seiyu; Massmart buyout and African exits; and increased PhonePe ownership during Flipkart separation. It describes intense omni-channel competition and factors affecting results, including economic, operational, climate, health, and cyber risks. It discusses inflation and supply-chain-driven inventory and cost pressures, pricing and merchandising responses that may affect margins, and continued economic and business uncertainty.

nodes.title: Company Performance Metrics
nodes.summary: The company’s financial framework centers on strong, efficient growth, operating discipline, and strategic capital allocation, with the goal of improving returns on capital. Growth priorities include productive opportunities, comparable store and club sales, Sam’s Club membership, Walmart+, eCommerce, and complementary omni-channel initiatives, alongside long-term investments. Comparable sales measure existing locations’ sales, including eCommerce; the company reports retail-calendar figures in quarterly releases but discusses fiscal-calendar figures here. U.S. comparable sales including fuel rose 8.2% in fiscal 2023 and 7.7% in 2022; Walmart U.S. rose 7.0% and 6.4%, respectively. The text also presents fiscal-year comparable-sales and fuel-impact figures for Walmart U.S., Sam’s Club, and total U.S.

nodes.title: Strong, Efficient Growth
nodes.summary: The text outlines Walmart’s competitive and macroeconomic risks, including labor, climate events, pandemics, inflation, supply chains, consumer conditions, and cybersecurity. It describes inflation and supply disruptions and the pricing and merchandising responses that may affect margins, alongside continued business uncertainty. It presents the financial framework of efficient growth, operating discipline, and strategic capital allocation; defines comparable sales and reports fiscal 2023/2022 U.S. and Sam’s Club results, drivers, and eCommerce contributions. It also discusses expense leverage and the effects of legal, restructuring, COVID-19, and wage costs; capital expenditure priorities; and returns measured by ROA, ROI, free cash flow, share repurchases, and dividends.

nodes.title: Sales Growth, Operating Discipline, and Capital Allocation
nodes.summary: The page describes fiscal 2023 and 2022 comparable-sales growth at Walmart U.S. and Sam’s Club, driven by transactions, average tickets, stimulus-supported spending, and inflation; eCommerce contributions and tobacco removal are also noted. It explains expense-management practices and reports sales, operating expenses, and expense ratios, including the effects of legal settlements, restructuring, COVID-related costs, and wage investments. It also outlines capital-allocation priorities and expenditures, favoring supply chain, customer initiatives, technology, and remodels over new openings.

nodes.title: Returns
key_items: Return on Assets and Return on Investment
nodes.summary: Walmart expects returns on capital to improve and discusses asset returns, free cash flow, share repurchases, and dividends. ROA (GAAP) fell from 5.6% in fiscal 2022 to 4.6% in 2023, mainly due to lower income; ROI (non-GAAP) declined from 14.9% to 12.7%, reflecting lower operating income and legal, reorganization, and restructuring charges. The text defines and reconciles ROA and ROI, explains ROI’s purpose and comparability limits, and provides underlying balance-sheet figures. Free cash flow is defined as operating cash flow less property and equipment payments; it rose to $12.0 billion in 2023 from $11.1 billion in 2022, after $25.8 billion in 2021. Operating cash flow and free cash flow trends are explained, including inventory, income, payment timing, and capital spending effects. The text notes free cash flow’s limitations and reconciles it to operating cash flow, while also reporting investing and financing cash flows.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Reports Walmart’s consolidated and segment results for fiscal 2023, 2022, and 2021, including revenues, sales, comparable sales, gross margins, operating income, net income, EPS, unit counts, and retail space. Explains consolidated revenue and margin changes, operating expenses, debt extinguishment, investment and disposition gains/losses, and effective tax-rate drivers. Details Walmart U.S., International, and Sam’s Club sales and operating performance, including inflation, customer spending, e-commerce, currency effects, U.K./Japan divestitures, restructuring, supply-chain costs, wages, COVID-related costs, membership income, and fuel impacts; notes the purpose of Sam’s Club’s fuel-excluded data and the basis for unit-count reporting.

nodes.title: Liquidity and Capital Resources Liquidity
Cash Equivalents and Working Capital Deficit
nodes.summary: The company expects operating cash flow, debt and borrowing capacity to fund operations, global investments, dividends and repurchases for at least 12 months and the foreseeable future. Operating cash flow was $28.8 billion in fiscal 2023, up from $24.2 billion in 2022 but below $36.1 billion in 2021; changes reflected inventory purchasing, operating income, and payment timing. Cash fell to $8.6 billion in 2023 from $14.8 billion in 2022, while the working capital deficit grew to $16.5 billion from $6.3 billion, mainly due to lower cash and higher accrued liabilities. The company attributes its usual deficit to efficient cash use, capital-market access and shareholder returns. Intercompany financing and repatriations help manage cash; foreign repatriations are generally free of U.S. federal tax, and restricted foreign cash was $2.9 billion in 2023 versus $4.3 billion in 2022, with no material liquidity impact expected. Investing cash outflows were $17.7 billion in 2023, $6.0 billion in 2022 and $10.1 billion in 2021, primarily for capital expenditures. The 2023 increase reflected prior-year U.K. and Japan divestiture proceeds and higher investment spending; the 2022 decrease reflected those proceeds, partly offset by capital expenditures.

nodes.title: Capital expenditures
nodes.summary: Fiscal 2024 capital expenditures are projected at $17–18 billion, focused on technology, supply chain, and customer initiatives. The text reports financing cash outflows for fiscal 2021–2023 and explains year-over-year changes, primarily involving debt repayments, early-extinguishment premiums, stock repurchases, debt issuance, and subsidiary equity funding. Fiscal 2023 included buyouts of Massmart and Alert Innovation; fiscal 2022 included Flipkart equity funding that reduced Walmart’s ownership. It also details short-term borrowing use, historical balances and rates, $0.4 billion outstanding at January 31, 2023 and 2022, available U.S. and international credit facilities, and letters of credit, including amounts drawn.

nodes.title: Short-term Borrowings
nodes.summary: The text reviews Walmart’s fiscal 2021–2023 investing and financing cash flows, their year-over-year drivers, capital expenditure plans, and fiscal 2024 investment priorities. It covers subsidiary stock transactions, short-term borrowing levels, credit facilities and letters of credit, long-term debt changes and estimated interest, dividend history and fiscal 2024 payment dates, and share-repurchase authorization and activity. It also identifies major operating and contractual cash requirements, including inventory, labor, taxes, legal settlements, debt, leases, subsidiary stock purchases, and other obligations.

nodes.title: Debt, Dividends, Repurchases, and Cash Requirements
nodes.summary: The page details fiscal 2023 long-term debt changes, the $1.2 billion increase, and estimated interest payments. It reports dividend payments for fiscal 2021–2023 and the fiscal 2024 dividend amount, increase, and payment dates. It describes the authorized share repurchase programs, remaining authorization, decision factors and funding, and shares, average prices, and amounts repurchased in fiscal 2021–2023. It also outlines operating and other material cash requirements and references relevant financial-statement notes.

nodes.title: Material Cash Requirements
nodes.summary: The text reports fiscal 2023 long-term debt movements: debt rose $1.2 billion, mainly from a September 2022 issuance, partly offset by maturities; estimated interest payments total $18.8 billion, including $1.7 billion in fiscal 2024. It summarizes dividends paid in fiscal 2021–2023 and the increased fiscal 2024 dividend and payment dates. It describes the new $20 billion share-repurchase authorization, remaining capacity, decision factors, funding expectations, and annual shares, prices, and amounts repurchased. Finally, it outlines operating and contractual cash requirements, including $33.3 billion in unrecorded purchase obligations ($11.6 billion due within one year), their scope and exclusions, and factors affecting payment timing and amounts.

The section reviews liquidity, cash flows, working capital, foreign cash and repatriation, and funding for operations, investments and shareholder returns. It covers investing and financing cash-flow trends, capital expenditure plans, subsidiary stock transactions, short- and long-term debt, borrowing facilities and letters of credit, estimated interest, dividends, and share-repurchase authorizations and activity. It also outlines operating and contractual cash requirements, including purchase obligations, inventory, labor, taxes, legal settlements, debt, leases and other commitments.

nodes.title: Capital Resources
nodes.summary: The company expects operating cash flows, cash on hand, short-term borrowings and capital-market access to cover anticipated needs and obligations, including seasonal inventory, capital spending, acquisitions, dividends and share repurchases. Its January 31, 2023 commercial-paper ratings were S&P A-1+, Moody’s P-1 and Fitch F1+; long-term debt ratings were AA, Aa2 and AA, respectively. Ratings may change based on operating, economic, industry, financial or strategic factors. Ratings are not investment recommendations, may be revised or withdrawn, and apply specifically to each security.

nodes.title: Other Matters
nodes.summary: The report’s Note 10 and Legal Proceedings sections describe opioid litigation and settlement matters, opioid-related securities and derivative actions, Asda Equal Value Claims and related indemnification, money-transfer services matters involving an FTC complaint and a federal investigation of fraud prevention and anti-money-laundering compliance, foreign direct investment matters, and a California environmental matter. These and other reported matters are contingent liabilities that may or may not result in material liability when resolved.

nodes.title: Summary of Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: Management explains that U.S. GAAP financial statements require estimates and judgments that are regularly reviewed and may differ from actual results. Critical estimates cover inventory valuation using retail or weighted-average LIFO methods and inflation provisions; valuation and annual impairment testing of indefinite-lived acquired intangibles; quarterly assessment, accrual, and disclosure of legal and regulatory contingencies; and income taxes, including uncertain tax positions, audits, deferred tax asset recoverability, valuation allowances, and changing laws and circumstances. Changes in assumptions or adverse outcomes may materially affect results.

summary: Explains Walmart’s fiscal 2021–2023 performance, metrics, segment results, and financial condition. Equity investment losses were $1.7 billion; recurring-fair-value holdings totaled $10.7 billion, with a 10% stock-price move implying a $1.1 billion value change.

Auditors tested related controls, reviewed board records and legal correspondence, consulted counsel, evaluated settlement assumptions and payments, and assessed disclosures. EY also opines Walmart’s internal financial reporting controls were effective in all material respects under COSO criteria, describes management and auditor responsibilities and audit procedures, and explains the purpose and inherent limitations of such controls. nodes.title: Walmart Internal Control Audit Opinion

The report explains management’s responsibility, the auditors’ PCAOB independence and audit responsibilities, and procedures used to assess risks, test control design and operating effectiveness, and obtain reasonable assurance.

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: The text defines internal control over financial reporting, its objectives and inherent limitations, and includes Ernst & Young’s dated signature. nodes.title: Note 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
Walmart Accounting Policies and Balances
nodes.summary: Walmart describes its omnichannel retail business and three reportable segments. Its consolidated statements include subsidiaries, eliminate intercompany items, consolidate qualifying variable-interest entities, and use the equity method for significant-influence investments; most non-U.S. operations are reported on a one-month lag. U.S. GAAP statements rely on estimates, so actual results may differ. Cash equivalents include investments with maturities of three months or less and card or electronic transactions settling within seven days; the page reports cash balances, foreign-held cash, and funds restricted from transfer to the U.S. Receivables, net of doubtful-account reserves, arise from customers, banks, suppliers, governments, and real estate transactions, with customer receivables reported for both years.

nodes.title: Inventory, Property, Equipment, and Lease Policies
nodes.summary: The page describes inventory valuation methods by business segment, including RIM, weighted-average cost, FIFO, and LIFO, with quarterly LIFO estimates adjusted to year-end results. Property and equipment are recorded at cost; improvements are capitalized, repairs expensed, and assets depreciated over estimated useful lives. It provides 2023 and 2022 asset balances and net values, leasehold depreciation rules, and depreciation and amortization expenses for 2023–2021. Lease accounting covers identification, discounted ROU assets and obligations, borrowing-rate assumptions, lease terms and short-term exemptions, and combining lease and non-lease components, including variable expenses.

nodes.title: Asset Impairment, Goodwill, and Fair Value
key_items: Goodwill and Other Acquired Intangible Assets
nodes.summary: The page explains impairment reviews for long-lived assets, goodwill and acquired intangible asset recognition, allocation, amortization, and impairment testing. It identifies the Company’s reporting units, reports goodwill balances and activity for fiscal 2022–2023, and notes indefinite-lived intangible balances and no significant intangible impairments. It defines fair value for assets and liabilities and describes equity investment accounting and fair-value-related gains and losses for fiscal 2021–2023.

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.summary: The text explains Walmart’s accounting policies and disclosures for long-lived asset impairment; goodwill and acquired intangible asset recognition, amortization, impairment testing, reporting units, goodwill movements, balances and charges; fair-value definitions; equity and debt investments and related gains or losses; divestiture indemnification liabilities and potential payments; self-insurance reserves and coverage; and derivative use, counterparty risks, collateral, balance-sheet presentation and hedge accounting. It also describes fair-value interest-rate swaps hedging fixed-rate debt and cross-currency swaps hedging forecasted debt payments, including accounting treatment and maturities.

nodes.title: Investments, Indemnifications, and Self-Insurance
nodes.summary: Certain investments are carried at cost with adjustments for observable price changes or impairment; trading debt securities are measured at fair value, with changes recognized in income. Trading securities totaled $0.5 billion in 2023 and $1.0 billion in 2022. Divestiture indemnities are recorded at estimated fair value; legal liabilities were $0.6 billion and $0.7 billion, respectively, with potential payments up to $3.1 billion. The Company estimates and regularly reviews undiscounted self-insurance reserves for claims and administration costs, and limits some exposures through insurance, including stop-loss coverage.

nodes.title: Derivatives
key_items: Fair Value Hedges; Cash Flow Hedges
nodes.summary: The text explains the Company’s derivative risk management, counterparty controls, collateral and netting practices, hedge-accounting rules, and accounting for fair value, cash flow, and divested-operation net investment hedges. It describes deferred and uncertain income tax accounting, redeemable noncontrolling-interest measurement and a Walmart U.S. acquisition put option, and revenue recognition for merchandise, services, eCommerce, and memberships, including membership revenue amounts for fiscal 2021–2023 and deferred revenue presentation.

nodes.title: Hedge Accounting, Income Taxes, and Redeemable Interests
nodes.summary: The page describes net investment hedges for divested U.K. and Japan operations, including how hedge gains and losses were recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and released upon sale. It outlines income tax accounting, deferred tax measurement and valuation allowances, tax provisions, and uncertain tax benefits, interest, and penalties. It also explains the presentation and remeasurement of redeemable noncontrolling interests and notes a Walmart U.S. interest subject to a put option beginning in December 2027.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition

nodes.summary: The text outlines the Company’s accounting policies for sales, membership fees, gift cards, services, cost of sales, supplier payments, operating expenses, advertising, and currency translation. It gives membership and advertising revenue figures for fiscal 2021–2023, explains where related amounts are reported and how unredeemed gift cards are estimated, and notes that distribution-cost classification can limit gross-profit comparisons with other retailers. It also describes a new FASB supplier-finance disclosure standard, its effective dates and transition rules, and management’s ongoing impact assessment.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition and Operating Expense Policies
key_items: Operating, Selling, General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.summary: Gift card sales are recognized upon redemption, with estimated unredeemed balances recognized as membership and other income over expected redemption periods; service revenue is recognized when performed. Cost of sales includes product, transportation and certain warehousing costs, reduced by supplier payments. Supplier consideration generally reduces cost of sales when inventory sells, except reimbursements of qualifying costs. Operating expenses include other operating costs, and differing distribution-cost classifications can limit gross-profit comparability. Advertising is expensed as incurred ( $4.1 billion, $3.9 billion and $3.2 billion in fiscal 2023, 2022 and 2021). International assets and liabilities use period-end exchange rates, with adjustments in accumulated other comprehensive loss; income statements use average rates.

The note summarizes Walmart’s business, segments, consolidation and equity-method policies, estimates, cash and receivables; inventory valuation; property, equipment and lease accounting; long-lived asset, goodwill and intangible impairment; fair-value and investment accounting; divestiture indemnities and self-insurance; and derivative risks and hedge accounting. It also covers income and deferred taxes, uncertain tax positions, redeemable noncontrolling interests, and revenue recognition for merchandise, services, eCommerce, memberships and gift cards, plus supplier payments, cost of sales, operating expenses, advertising, currency translation and a new supplier-finance disclosure standard.

nodes.title: Note 4. Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss
nodes.summary: The note presents fiscal 2021–2023 changes in accumulated other comprehensive loss, by currency translation and other, net investment hedges, cash flow hedges, and minimum pension liability, including opening and closing balances, unrealized changes, and reclassifications. Reclassified foreign-currency bond and derivative amounts are recorded in interest, net; pension and business-disposition translation amounts are recorded in other gains and losses. Expected derivative reclassifications over the next 12 months are not significant.

nodes.title: Note 5. Accrued Liabilities
nodes.summary: As of January 31, 2023 and 2022, accrued liabilities totaled $31.126 billion and $26.060 billion, respectively. Categories include accrued wages and benefits; self-insurance; non-income taxes; the opioid litigation settlement; deferred gift card revenue; and other liabilities. Wages and benefits cover salaries, vacation, bonuses, and incentive plans; self-insurance covers workers’ compensation, liability, product, and certain healthcare obligations; taxes include payroll, property, value-added, sales, and other taxes. The opioid balance is the remaining settlement amount. Other items include deferred membership revenue, PhonePe stock purchase, interest, supply chain, advertising, and maintenance and utilities.

nodes.title: Note 6. Short-term Borrowings and Long-term Debt
nodes.summary: The note details short-term borrowings, committed credit facilities, letters of credit, and long-term debt balances and terms for 2023 and 2022, including rates, maturities, covenants, and debt categories. It lists upcoming annual maturities and fiscal 2023 note issuances, their terms and proceeds, and states the notes are senior unsecured obligations without dividend or repurchase restrictions. It also summarizes fiscal 2023 matured-debt repayments, fiscal 2022 repayments and extinguishments, and a $2.4 billion fiscal 2022 extinguishment loss, including $2.3 billion of early-redemption premiums.

nodes.title: Note 7. Leases
nodes.summary: The Company leases retail, distribution, fulfillment, warehouse, office, land, and equipment assets in the U.S. and internationally. The note reports operating, finance (right-of-use asset amortization and interest), and variable lease costs for fiscal 2021–2023; lease-related cash payments and assets obtained in exchange for obligations over those years; and 2023 weighted-average lease terms and discount rates. It also presents operating and finance lease obligations by fiscal year from 2024 onward, total undiscounted obligations, imputed interest, and net obligations as of January 31, 2023.

nodes.title: Note 8. Fair Value Measurements
key_items: Derivatives; Nonrecurring Fair Value Measurements; Other Fair Value Disclosures
nodes.summary: The note explains the fair value hierarchy (Levels 1–3) and reports recurring fair values of equity investments: $10.669 billion in 2023 and $11.888 billion in 2022. It describes Level 2 derivative valuation using interest-rate and currency curves and provides swap notionals and fair values, noting amounts are primarily classified in deferred income taxes and other. Nonrecurring measurements include 2022 impairment charges of $0.4 billion on U.K. and Japan operations and 2021 Level 3 disposal-group impairments within an $8.3 billion pretax divestiture loss, including a $2.3 billion Asda pension charge; no material nonrecurring balances existed in 2023. Cash and short-term borrowings’ carrying values approximate fair value; long-term debt is carried at cost and valued with Level 2 inputs, with carrying/fair values of $38.840/$38.169 billion in 2023 and $37.667/$42.381 billion in 2022.

nodes.title: Deferred Taxes
nodes.summary: The text details deferred tax assets, liabilities, valuation allowances, and balance-sheet classification for 2023 and 2022. It explains that roughly $3 billion of deferred tax liabilities on indefinitely reinvested foreign earnings remain unrecorded. It reports $32.3 billion in loss carryforwards, their expiration profile, how deferred-tax-asset realizability and valuation allowances are assessed, and allowance balances and activity. nodes.title: Deferred Taxes and Carryforwards
key_items: Net Operating Losses, Tax Credit Carryforwards and Valuation Allowances
nodes.summary: The page presents deferred tax balance-sheet classifications and net deferred tax liabilities for 2023 and 2022. It explains that most previously unremitted foreign earnings were taxed under the 2017 Tax Act, while about $3 billion of deferred tax liabilities on indefinitely reinvested earnings remain unrecorded. As of 2023, net operating and capital loss carryforwards totaled $32.3 billion, with $19.6 billion expiring through 2043 and the rest having no expiration. The company assesses deferred tax asset recoverability using expected taxable income and tax strategies, records valuation allowances when recovery is not more likely than not, and reported allowances of $7.8 billion in 2023 and $9.5 billion in 2022; 2023 activity included builds and releases from expirations.

nodes.title: Uncertain Tax Positions
nodes.summary: The Company recognizes uncertain tax benefits only when it is more likely than not they will withstand tax-authority challenge. Gross unrecognized benefits for continuing operations were $3.3 billion in 2023 and $3.2 billion in 2022; amounts affecting the effective tax rate were $1.5 billion and $1.8 billion, respectively. nodes.title: Note 11. Retirement-Related Benefits
nodes.summary: The Company’s U.S. 401(k) plan allows contributions upon hire; Puerto Rico’s plan generally allows them after one year. After one year, both match 100% of contributions up to 6% of eligible earnings, immediately vested; participants may contribute up to 50% of pretax earnings subject to statutory limits. Non-U.S. international associates participate in locally regulated defined contribution plans. Contribution expenses for fiscal 2023, 2022 and 2021 are presented by U.S. and international plans. The former U.K. subsidiary Asda’s defined benefit plan received a $1.0 billion contribution in fiscal 2020 to purchase bulk annuity coverage and release future obligations; on Asda’s sale, $2.3 billion of accumulated pension components entered the disposal group, with an estimated pretax loss recognized in fiscal 2021.

nodes.title: Note 12. Disposals, Acquisitions and Related Items
nodes.summary: The note describes Walmart International divestitures. Walmart deconsolidated Asda, retaining a debt security and certain legal and tax liabilities. Seiyu was sold in March 2021 for $1.2 billion, with a $0.2 billion closing loss and a prior $1.9 billion held-for-sale loss; Walmart retained a 15% equity interest. Walmart Argentina was sold in November 2020, resulting in a $1.0 billion fiscal 2021 loss, mainly from cumulative currency translation losses. Other immaterial transactions also occurred.

nodes.title: Note 13. Segments and Disaggregated Revenue
nodes.summary: The note describes Walmart’s three reportable segments—U.S., International and Sam’s Club—their operations, CODM oversight, performance measures and corporate support, and presents segment financial results for fiscal 2021–2023, including sales, operating income, assets, expenses and tax reconciliation. It reports U.S. and non-U.S. revenues and long-lived assets, noting no material individual foreign country or customer and excluding held-for-sale assets. nodes.summary: Common Stock shares are fully paid and non-assessable when issued for legally permissible consideration at least equal to par value; holders have no liability for company obligations. Each share carries one vote, with ordinary matters decided by majority vote, contested director elections by plurality, and specified major corporate actions requiring majority approval; cumulative voting is absent. Anti-Takeover Provisions of Delaware Law, Our Certificate and Our Bylaws
nodes.summary: The Certificate and Bylaws contain provisions that may delay or deter control changes, including board authority to fill vacancies and newly created seats, advance notice and enhanced disclosure requirements for shareholder nominations and proposals, authority to issue up to 100 million preferred shares with board-determined terms, and amendment by shareholders or directors. Delaware DGCL Section 203 generally bars business combinations for three years with 15%-or-more interested stockholders and their affiliates or associates, subject to specified prior board approval, 85% ownership, or later board and two-thirds disinterested-stockholder approval exceptions. The Certificate also makes Delaware’s Court of Chancery the exclusive forum for specified stockholder claims, unless the Company agrees in writing to another forum.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF DEBT SECURITIES
Notes, Ranking, and Trustee
nodes.summary: Summarizes the Notes under the 2005 Indenture with BNYM, governed by New York law, which permits unlimited issuance and additional pari passu securities without holder consent. The €650 million Notes were issued April 8, 2014, mature April 8, 2026, bear 2.550% annual interest, and had €650 million outstanding as of January 31, 2023. They are senior unsecured obligations ranking equally with other unsecured, unsubordinated debt; subsidiaries neither guarantee nor owe them, and may incur debt without restriction. BNYM is trustee and paying agent, and has existing and potential future banking relationships with the Company.

nodes.title: Payment on the Notes
nodes.summary: Notes’ principal (including redemption), accrued interest, and additional amounts are payable in euros. If euros become unavailable due to exchange controls or other circumstances beyond the issuer’s control, or cease to be used by euro-area member states or for relevant public or international banking transactions, payments switch to U.S. dollars until euros are available or used again. The conversion rate is the Federal Reserve-mandated rate at the close of business two Business Days before payment; if none is mandated, use the latest Wall Street Journal euro-dollar rate available by then. Dollar payments do not constitute default. A Business Day excludes weekends and days when banks in New York City or London are closed by law or executive order, and requires TARGET2 (or its successor) to be open.

nodes.title: Payment of Additional Amounts
nodes.summary: The issuer generally pays Note principal and interest without U.S. tax withholding, and grosses up payments to eligible Non-U.S. beneficial owners when withholding is legally required. Additional amounts are excluded for specified cases, including U.S. connections, late presentation, certain taxes or tax statuses, non-withholding taxes, avoidable paying-agent withholding, failure to provide required tax documentation (including FATCA), certain 10% shareholders or related controlled foreign corporations, EU savings-tax withholding, and combinations of these exclusions. Fiduciaries and partnerships receive no more than their underlying beneficiaries or members would qualify for. The text defines “Non-U.S. Person.”

nodes.title: Redemption for Tax Reasons
nodes.summary: The issuer may optionally redeem all, but not part, of the Notes if a change or proposed change in U.S. tax laws, treaties, regulations, rulings, or their official application, enforcement, or interpretation causes—or, based on an independent counsel’s written opinion, will cause—the issuer to owe additional amounts. Redemption requires 30–60 days’ prior notice and is at 100% of principal plus any accrued and unpaid interest through the redemption date.

nodes.title: Optional Redemption
nodes.summary: The issuer may redeem Notes in whole or part at any time. Before January 8, 2026, the price is the greater of par or the present value of remaining scheduled principal and interest (excluding accrued interest), discounted using Actual/Actual (ICMA) at the Comparable Government Bond Rate plus 15 basis points; accrued unpaid interest is added in either case. On or after that date, redemption is at par plus accrued unpaid interest. Interest installments due on or before redemption remain payable on their payment dates to holders of record. The definitions specify how an independent investment bank selects an appropriate German government bond and calculates the Comparable Government Bond Rate using market prices and yields three Business Days before redemption.

nodes.title: Covenants
key_items: Consolidation, Merger and Sale of Assets
nodes.summary: The Indenture’s limited covenants do not restrict the Company’s or subsidiaries’ debt or lease obligations, lien-secured debt, or dividends, distributions, and stock repurchases or redemptions. The Company may merge, consolidate, reorganize, amalgamate, or transfer substantially all assets if a U.S.-organized successor assumes the Notes and Indenture obligations, no continuing event of default results, and other Indenture conditions are met. The successor assumes the Company’s rights and powers, and a compliant transaction is not a default or event of default.

nodes.title: Events of Default
nodes.summary: Events of default include overdue interest (30 days), principal or premium, uncured covenant or warranty breaches after notice (90 days), bankruptcy or insolvency events, and series-specific defaults; defaults may affect only one series. For non-bankruptcy defaults, the trustee or holders of 25% may accelerate that series; bankruptcy defaults automatically accelerate all series. A majority may rescind acceleration under stated conditions. The issuer must annually report defaults. Individual holders generally may sue only after notice, a 25% request, indemnity, trustee inaction for 60 days, and no contrary majority direction; proceedings benefit holders equally. A series majority directs remedies and may waive defaults, while the trustee must act prudently. Individual holders retain the right to sue for overdue payments or redemption/repurchase amounts.

nodes.title: Modification and Waivers
nodes.summary: Indenture amendments generally require consent from holders of a majority of affected Notes, while changes to specified payment, maturity, currency, enforcement, voting-threshold, and amendment-protection terms require each affected holder’s consent. The issuer and trustee may make listed non-adverse or administrative amendments without holder consent, including succession, added covenants or defaults, corrections, new series, trustee changes, and SEC compliance. Majority holders may waive acceleration and rescind it if other defaults are resolved and required payments made; they may also waive most past defaults, but not uncured payment defaults or provisions requiring unanimous consent. The trustee may act to protect holders following a continuing default, subject to majority request, indemnity, and other conditions.

nodes.title: Discharge, Legal Defeasance and Covenant Defeasance
nodes.summary: The issuer may elect legal defeasance, discharging obligations on outstanding Notes while preserving holders’ payment rights, specified administrative and trustee obligations, and the Indenture’s discharge provisions. Alternatively, covenant defeasance releases covenant obligations other than payment, so their breach is no longer a default. Either option requires a sufficient irrevocable deposit of cash, government securities, or both; no disqualifying default; tax and bankruptcy-related legal opinions; and, for covenant defeasance, a first-priority lien for holders. Legal defeasance may follow covenant defeasance.

nodes.title: Book-Entry and Settlement
nodes.summary: The Notes are issued in book-entry form as global notes held by a common depositary for Clearstream and Euroclear and registered to the depositary or its nominee. Beneficial interests and their transfers are recorded only through those systems; certificated Notes are generally not issued in exchange, except as described elsewhere.

nodes.title: Certificated Notes
nodes.summary: Global Notes may be exchanged for certificated Notes with the same terms in authorized denominations if the depositary cannot continue and no successor is appointed within 90 days, the issuer discontinues the book-entry system, or a continuing event of default occurs. Certificated Notes are registered in names directed by the common depositary. Otherwise, a Global Note may only be exchanged for another Global Note of the same aggregate denomination registered to the common depositary or its nominee.
